title: Notes from the Underground
text: I am a sick man....

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I am a spiteful man. I am an unattractive man. I believe my liver is diseased.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: However, I know nothing at all about my disease, and do not know for certain what ails me. I don’t consult a doctor for it, and never have, though I have a respect for medicine and doctors.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Besides, I am extremely superstitious, sufficiently so to respect medicine, anyway (I am well-educated enough not to be superstitious, but I am superstitious).

title: Notes from the Underground
text: No, I refuse to consult a doctor from spite.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: That you probably will not understand.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Well, I understand it, though.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Of course, I can’t explain who it is precisely that I am mortifying in this case by my spite: I am perfectly well aware that I cannot “pay out” the doctors by not consulting them; I know better than anyone that by all this I am only injuring myself and no one else.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But still, if I don’t consult a doctor it is from spite.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: My liver is bad, well—let it get worse!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I have been going on like that for a long time—twenty years.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Now I am forty.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I used to be in the government service, but am no longer.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I was a spiteful official.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I was rude and took pleasure in being so.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I did not take bribes, you see, so I was bound to find a recompense in that, at least.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: (A poor jest, but I will not scratch it out. I wrote it thinking it would sound very witty; but now that I have seen myself that I only wanted to show off in a despicable way, I will not scratch it out on purpose!)

title: Notes from the Underground
text: When petitioners used to come for information to the table at which I sat, I used to grind my teeth at them, and felt intense enjoyment when I succeeded in making anybody unhappy.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I almost did succeed.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: For the most part they were all timid people—of course, they were petitioners.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But of the uppish ones there was one officer in particular I could not endure.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: He simply would not be humble, and clanked his sword in a disgusting way.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I carried on a feud with him for eighteen months over that sword.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: At last I got the better of him.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: He left off clanking it.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: That happened in my youth, though.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But do you know, gentlemen, what was the chief point about my spite?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Why, the whole point, the real sting of it lay in the fact that continually, even in the moment of the acutest spleen, I was inwardly conscious with shame that I was not only not a spiteful but not even an embittered man, that I was simply scaring sparrows at random and amusing myself by it.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I might foam at the mouth, but bring me a doll to play with, give me a cup of tea with sugar in it, and maybe I should be appeased.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I might even be genuinely touched, though probably I should grind my teeth at myself afterwards and lie awake at night with shame for months after.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: That was my way.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I was lying when I said just now that I was a spiteful official.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I was lying from spite.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I was simply amusing myself with the petitioners and with the officer, and in reality I never could become spiteful.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I was conscious every moment in myself of many, very many elements absolutely opposite to that.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I felt them positively swarming in me, these opposite elements.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I knew that they had been swarming in me all my life and craving some outlet from me, but I would not let them, would not let them, purposely would not let them come out.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: They tormented me till I was ashamed: they drove me to convulsions and—sickened me, at last, how they sickened me!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Now, are not you fancying, gentlemen, that I am expressing remorse for something now, that I am asking your forgiveness for something?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I am sure you are fancying that ...

title: Notes from the Underground
text: However, I assure you I do not care if you are....

title: Notes from the Underground
text: It was not only that I could not become spiteful, I did not know how to become anything; neither spiteful nor kind, neither a rascal nor an honest man, neither a hero nor an insect.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Now, I am living out my life in my corner, taunting myself with the spiteful and useless consolation that an intelligent man cannot become anything seriously, and it is only the fool who becomes anything.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Yes, a man in the nineteenth century must and morally ought to be pre-eminently a characterless creature; a man of character, an active man is pre-eminently a limited creature.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: That is my conviction of forty years.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I am forty years old now, and you know forty years is a whole lifetime; you know it is extreme old age.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: To live longer than forty years is bad manners, is vulgar, immoral.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Who does live beyond forty?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Answer that, sincerely and honestly I will tell you who do: fools and worthless fellows.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I tell all old men that to their face, all these venerable old men, all these silver-haired and reverend seniors!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I tell the whole world that to its face!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I have a right to say so, for I shall go on living to sixty myself.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: To seventy!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: To eighty!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Stay, let me take breath ...

title: Notes from the Underground
text: You imagine no doubt, gentlemen, that I want to amuse you.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: You are mistaken in that, too.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I am by no means such a mirthful person as you imagine, or as you may imagine; however, irritated by all this babble (and I feel that you are irritated) you think fit to ask me who I am—then my answer is, I am a collegiate assessor.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I was in the service that I might have something to eat (and solely for that reason), and when last year a distant relation left me six thousand roubles in his will I immediately retired from the service and settled down in my corner.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I used to live in this corner before, but now I have settled down in it.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: My room is a wretched, horrid one in the outskirts of the town.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: My servant is an old country-woman, ill-natured from stupidity, and, moreover, there is always a nasty smell about her.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I am told that the Petersburg climate is bad for me, and that with my small means it is very expensive to live in Petersburg.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I know all that better than all these sage and experienced counsellors and monitors....

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But I am remaining in Petersburg; I am not going away from Petersburg!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I am not going away because ... ech!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Why, it is absolutely no matter whether I am going away or not going away.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But what can a decent man speak of with most pleasure?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Answer: Of himself.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Well, so I will talk about myself.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I want now to tell you, gentlemen, whether you care to hear it or not, why I could not even become an insect.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I tell you solemnly, that I have many times tried to become an insect.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But I was not equal even to that.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I swear, gentlemen, that to be too conscious is an illness—a real thorough-going illness.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: For man’s everyday needs, it would have been quite enough to have the ordinary human consciousness, that is, half or a quarter of the amount which falls to the lot of a cultivated man of our unhappy nineteenth century, especially one who has the fatal ill-luck to inhabit Petersburg, the most theoretical and intentional town on the whole terrestrial globe.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: (There are intentional and unintentional towns.)

title: Notes from the Underground
text: It would have been quite enough, for instance, to have the consciousness by which all so-called direct persons and men of action live.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I bet you think I am writing all this from affectation, to be witty at the expense of men of action; and what is more, that from ill-bred affectation, I am clanking a sword like my officer.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But, gentlemen, whoever can pride himself on his diseases and even swagger over them?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Though, after all, everyone does do that; people do pride themselves on their diseases, and I do, may be, more than anyone.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: We will not dispute it; my contention was absurd.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But yet I am firmly persuaded that a great deal of consciousness, every sort of consciousness, in fact, is a disease.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I stick to that.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Let us leave that, too, for a minute.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Tell me this: why does it happen that at the very, yes, at the very moments when I am most capable of feeling every refinement of all that is “sublime and beautiful,” as they used to say at one time, it would, as though of design, happen to me not only to feel but to do such ugly things, such that ...

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Well, in short, actions that all, perhaps, commit; but which, as though purposely, occurred to me at the very time when I was most conscious that they ought not to be committed.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: The more conscious I was of goodness and of all that was “sublime and beautiful,” the more deeply I sank into my mire and the more ready I was to sink in it altogether.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But the chief point was that all this was, as it were, not accidental in me, but as though it were bound to be so.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: It was as though it were my most normal condition, and not in the least disease or depravity, so that at last all desire in me to struggle against this depravity passed.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: It ended by my almost believing (perhaps actually believing) that this was perhaps my normal condition.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But at first, in the beginning, what agonies I endured in that struggle!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I did not believe it was the same with other people, and all my life I hid this fact about myself as a secret.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I was ashamed (even now, perhaps, I am ashamed): I got to the point of feeling a sort of secret abnormal, despicable enjoyment in returning home to my corner on some disgusting Petersburg night, acutely conscious that that day I had committed a loathsome action again, that what was done could never be undone, and secretly, inwardly gnawing, gnawing at myself for it, tearing and consuming myself till at last the bitterness turned into a sort of shameful accursed sweetness, and at last—into positive real enjoyment!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Yes, into enjoyment, into enjoyment!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I insist upon that.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I have spoken of this because I keep wanting to know for a fact whether other people feel such enjoyment?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I will explain; the enjoyment was just from the too intense consciousness of one’s own degradation; it was from feeling oneself that one had reached the last barrier, that it was horrible, but that it could not be otherwise; that there was no escape for you; that you never could become a different man; that even if time and faith were still left you to change into something different you would most likely not wish to change; or if you did wish to, even then you would do nothing; because perhaps in reality there was nothing for you to change into.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: And the worst of it was, and the root of it all, that it was all in accord with the normal fundamental laws of over-acute consciousness, and with the inertia that was the direct result of those laws, and that consequently one was not only unable to change but could do absolutely nothing.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Thus it would follow, as the result of acute consciousness, that one is not to blame in being a scoundrel; as though that were any consolation to the scoundrel once he has come to realise that he actually is a scoundrel.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But enough....

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Ech, I have talked a lot of nonsense, but what have I explained?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: How is enjoyment in this to be explained?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But I will explain it.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I will get to the bottom of it!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: That is why I have taken up my pen....

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I, for instance, have a great deal of amour propre.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I am as suspicious and prone to take offence as a humpback or a dwarf.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But upon my word I sometimes have had moments when if I had happened to be slapped in the face I should, perhaps, have been positively glad of it.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I say, in earnest, that I should probably have been able to discover even in that a peculiar sort of enjoyment—the enjoyment, of course, of despair; but in despair there are the most intense enjoyments, especially when one is very acutely conscious of the hopelessness of one’s position.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: And when one is slapped in the face—why then the consciousness of being rubbed into a pulp would positively overwhelm one.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: The worst of it is, look at it which way one will, it still turns out that I was always the most to blame in everything.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: And what is most humiliating of all, to blame for no fault of my own but, so to say, through the laws of nature.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: In the first place, to blame because I am cleverer than any of the people surrounding me. (I have always considered myself cleverer than any of the people surrounding me, and sometimes, would you believe it, have been positively ashamed of it. At any rate, I have all my life, as it were, turned my eyes away and never could look people straight in the face.) To blame, finally, because even if I had had magnanimity, I should only have had more suffering from the sense of its uselessness.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I should certainly have never been able to do anything from being magnanimous—neither to forgive, for my assailant would perhaps have slapped me from the laws of nature, and one cannot forgive the laws of nature; nor to forget, for even if it were owing to the laws of nature, it is insulting all the same.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Finally, even if I had wanted to be anything but magnanimous, had desired on the contrary to revenge myself on my assailant, I could not have revenged myself on any one for anything because I should certainly never have made up my mind to do anything, even if I had been able to.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Why should I not have made up my mind?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: About that in particular I want to say a few words.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: With people who know how to revenge themselves and to stand up for themselves in general, how is it done?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Why, when they are possessed, let us suppose, by the feeling of revenge, then for the time there is nothing else but that feeling left in their whole being.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Such a gentleman simply dashes straight for his object like an infuriated bull with its horns down, and nothing but a wall will stop him.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: (By the way: facing the wall, such gentlemen—that is, the “direct” persons and men of action—are genuinely nonplussed. For them a wall is not an evasion, as for us people who think and consequently do nothing; it is not an excuse for turning aside, an excuse for which we are always very glad, though we scarcely believe in it ourselves, as a rule. No, they are nonplussed in all sincerity. The wall has for them something tranquillising, morally soothing, final—maybe even something mysterious ... but of the wall later.)

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Well, such a direct person I regard as the real normal man, as his tender mother nature wished to see him when she graciously brought him into being on the earth.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I envy such a man till I am green in the face.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: He is stupid.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I am not disputing that, but perhaps the normal man should be stupid, how do you know?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Perhaps it is very beautiful, in fact.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: And I am the more persuaded of that suspicion, if one can call it so, by the fact that if you take, for instance, the antithesis of the normal man, that is, the man of acute consciousness, who has come, of course, not out of the lap of nature but out of a retort (this is almost mysticism, gentlemen, but I suspect this, too), this retort-made man is sometimes so nonplussed in the presence of his antithesis that with all his exaggerated consciousness he genuinely thinks of himself as a mouse and not a man.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: It may be an acutely conscious mouse, yet it is a mouse, while the other is a man, and therefore, et caetera, et caetera.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: And the worst of it is, he himself, his very own self, looks on himself as a mouse; no one asks him to do so; and that is an important point.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Now let us look at this mouse in action.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Let us suppose, for instance, that it feels insulted, too (and it almost always does feel insulted), and wants to revenge itself, too.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: There may even be a greater accumulation of spite in it than in l’homme de la nature et de la vérité.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: The base and nasty desire to vent that spite on its assailant rankles perhaps even more nastily in it than in l’homme de la nature et de la vérité.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: For through his innate stupidity the latter looks upon his revenge as justice pure and simple; while in consequence of his acute consciousness the mouse does not believe in the justice of it.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: To come at last to the deed itself, to the very act of revenge.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Apart from the one fundamental nastiness the luckless mouse succeeds in creating around it so many other nastinesses in the form of doubts and questions, adds to the one question so many unsettled questions that there inevitably works up around it a sort of fatal brew, a stinking mess, made up of its doubts, emotions, and of the contempt spat upon it by the direct men of action who stand solemnly about it as judges and arbitrators, laughing at it till their healthy sides ache.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Of course the only thing left for it is to dismiss all that with a wave of its paw, and, with a smile of assumed contempt in which it does not even itself believe, creep ignominiously into its mouse-hole.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: There in its nasty, stinking, underground home our insulted, crushed and ridiculed mouse promptly becomes absorbed in cold, malignant and, above all, everlasting spite.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: For forty years together it will remember its injury down to the smallest, most ignominious details, and every time will add, of itself, details still more ignominious, spitefully teasing and tormenting itself with its own imagination.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: It will itself be ashamed of its imaginings, but yet it will recall it all, it will go over and over every detail, it will invent unheard of things against itself, pretending that those things might happen, and will forgive nothing.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Maybe it will begin to revenge itself, too, but, as it were, piecemeal, in trivial ways, from behind the stove, incognito, without believing either in its own right to vengeance, or in the success of its revenge, knowing that from all its efforts at revenge it will suffer a hundred times more than he on whom it revenges itself, while he, I daresay, will not even scratch himself.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: On its deathbed it will recall it all over again, with interest accumulated over all the years and ...

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But it is just in that cold, abominable half despair, half belief, in that conscious burying oneself alive for grief in the underworld for forty years, in that acutely recognised and yet partly doubtful hopelessness of one’s position, in that hell of unsatisfied desires turned inward, in that fever of oscillations, of resolutions determined for ever and repented of again a minute later—that the savour of that strange enjoyment of which I have spoken lies.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: It is so subtle, so difficult of analysis, that persons who are a little limited, or even simply persons of strong nerves, will not understand a single atom of it.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: “Possibly,” you will add on your own account with a grin, “people will not understand it either who have never received a slap in the face,” and in that way you will politely hint to me that I, too, perhaps, have had the experience of a slap in the face in my life, and so I speak as one who knows.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I bet that you are thinking that.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But set your minds at rest, gentlemen, I have not received a slap in the face, though it is absolutely a matter of indifference to me what you may think about it.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Possibly, I even regret, myself, that I have given so few slaps in the face during my life.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But enough ... not another word on that subject of such extreme interest to you.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I will continue calmly concerning persons with strong nerves who do not understand a certain refinement of enjoyment.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Though in certain circumstances these gentlemen bellow their loudest like bulls, though this, let us suppose, does them the greatest credit, yet, as I have said already, confronted with the impossible they subside at once.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: The impossible means the stone wall!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: What stone wall?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Why, of course, the laws of nature, the deductions of natural science, mathematics.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: As soon as they prove to you, for instance, that you are descended from a monkey, then it is no use scowling, accept it for a fact.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: When they prove to you that in reality one drop of your own fat must be dearer to you than a hundred thousand of your fellow-creatures, and that this conclusion is the final solution of all so-called virtues and duties and all such prejudices and fancies, then you have just to accept it, there is no help for it, for twice two is a law of mathematics.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Just try refuting it.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: “Upon my word, they will shout at you, it is no use protesting: it is a case of twice two makes four! Nature does not ask your permission, she has nothing to do with your wishes, and whether you like her laws or dislike them, you are bound to accept her as she is, and consequently all her conclusions. A wall, you see, is a wall ... and so on, and so on.”

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Merciful Heavens! but what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic, when, for some reason I dislike those laws and the fact that twice two makes four?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Of course I cannot break through the wall by battering my head against it if I really have not the strength to knock it down, but I am not going to be reconciled to it simply because it is a stone wall and I have not the strength.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: As though such a stone wall really were a consolation, and really did contain some word of conciliation, simply because it is as true as twice two makes four.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Oh, absurdity of absurdities!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: How much better it is to understand it all, to recognise it all, all the impossibilities and the stone wall; not to be reconciled to one of those impossibilities and stone walls if it disgusts you to be reconciled to it; by the way of the most inevitable, logical combinations to reach the most revolting conclusions on the everlasting theme, that even for the stone wall you are yourself somehow to blame, though again it is as clear as day you are not to blame in the least, and therefore grinding your teeth in silent impotence to sink into luxurious inertia, brooding on the fact that there is no one even for you to feel vindictive against, that you have not, and perhaps never will have, an object for your spite, that it is a sleight of hand, a bit of juggling, a card-sharper’s trick, that it is simply a mess, no knowing what and no knowing who, but in spite of all these uncertainties and jugglings, still there is an ache in you, and the more you do not know, the worse the ache.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: “Ha, ha, ha! You will be finding enjoyment in toothache next,” you cry, with a laugh.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: “Well, even in toothache there is enjoyment,” I answer.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I had toothache for a whole month and I know there is.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: In that case, of course, people are not spiteful in silence, but moan; but they are not candid moans, they are malignant moans, and the malignancy is the whole point.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: The enjoyment of the sufferer finds expression in those moans; if he did not feel enjoyment in them he would not moan.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: It is a good example, gentlemen, and I will develop it.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Those moans express in the first place all the aimlessness of your pain, which is so humiliating to your consciousness; the whole legal system of nature on which you spit disdainfully, of course, but from which you suffer all the same while she does not.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: They express the consciousness that you have no enemy to punish, but that you have pain; the consciousness that in spite of all possible Wagenheims you are in complete slavery to your teeth; that if someone wishes it, your teeth will leave off aching, and if he does not, they will go on aching another three months; and that finally if you are still contumacious and still protest, all that is left you for your own gratification is to thrash yourself or beat your wall with your fist as hard as you can, and absolutely nothing more.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Well, these mortal insults, these jeers on the part of someone unknown, end at last in an enjoyment which sometimes reaches the highest degree of voluptuousness.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I ask you, gentlemen, listen sometimes to the moans of an educated man of the nineteenth century suffering from toothache, on the second or third day of the attack, when he is beginning to moan, not as he moaned on the first day, that is, not simply because he has toothache, not just as any coarse peasant, but as a man affected by progress and European civilisation, a man who is “divorced from the soil and the national elements,” as they express it now-a-days.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: His moans become nasty, disgustingly malignant, and go on for whole days and nights.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: And of course he knows himself that he is doing himself no sort of good with his moans; he knows better than anyone that he is only lacerating and harassing himself and others for nothing; he knows that even the audience before whom he is making his efforts, and his whole family, listen to him with loathing, do not put a ha’porth of faith in him, and inwardly understand that he might moan differently, more simply, without trills and flourishes, and that he is only amusing himself like that from ill-humour, from malignancy.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Well, in all these recognitions and disgraces it is that there lies a voluptuous pleasure.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: As though he would say: “I am worrying you, I am lacerating your hearts, I am keeping everyone in the house awake.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Well, stay awake then, you, too, feel every minute that I have toothache.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I am not a hero to you now, as I tried to seem before, but simply a nasty person, an impostor.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Well, so be it, then!

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I am very glad that you see through me.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: It is nasty for you to hear my despicable moans: well, let it be nasty; here I will let you have a nastier flourish in a minute....

title: Notes from the Underground
text: You do not understand even now, gentlemen?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: No, it seems our development and our consciousness must go further to understand all the intricacies of this pleasure.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: You laugh?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Delighted.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: My jests, gentlemen, are of course in bad taste, jerky, involved, lacking self-confidence.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: But of course that is because I do not respect myself.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Can a man of perception respect himself at all?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: Come, can a man who attempts to find enjoyment in the very feeling of his own degradation possibly have a spark of respect for himself?

title: Notes from the Underground
text: I am not saying this now from any mawkish kind of remorse.

title: Notes from the Underground
text: And, indeed, I could never endure saying, “Forgive me, Papa, I won’t do it again,” not because I am incapable of saying that—on the contrary, perhaps just because I have been too capable of it, and in what a way, too.

You declare that you are afraid of nothing and at the same time try to ingratiate yourself in our good opinion. But how much is your love worth now? You are sold, all of you, body and soul, and there is no need to strive for love when you can have everything without love. And you know there is no greater insult to a girl than that, do you understand? To be sure, I have heard that they comfort you, poor fools, they let you have lovers of your own here. But you know that’s simply a farce, that’s simply a sham, it’s just laughing at you, and you are taken in by it! Why, do you suppose he really loves you, that lover of yours? I don’t believe it. How can he love you when he knows you may be called away from him any minute? He would be a low fellow if he did! Will he have a grain of respect for you? What have you in common with him? He laughs at you and robs you—that is all his love amounts to! You are lucky if he does not beat you. Very likely he does beat you, too. Ask him, if you have got one, whether he will marry you. He will laugh in your face, if he doesn’t spit in it or give you a blow—though maybe he is not worth a bad halfpenny himself. And for what have you ruined your life, if you come to think of it? For the coffee they give you to drink and the plentiful meals? But with what object are they feeding you up? An honest girl couldn’t swallow the food, for she would know what she was being fed for. You are in debt here, and, of course, you will always be in debt, and you will go on in debt to the end, till the visitors here begin to scorn you. And that will soon happen, don’t rely upon your youth—all that flies by express train here, you know. You will be kicked out. And not simply kicked out; long before that she’ll begin nagging at you, scolding you, abusing you, as though you had not sacrificed your health for her, had not thrown away your youth and your soul for her benefit, but as though you had ruined her, beggared her, robbed her. And don’t expect anyone to take your part: the others, your companions, will attack you, too, win her favour, for all are in slavery here, and have lost all conscience and pity here long ago. They have become utterly vile, and nothing on earth is viler, more loathsome, and more insulting than their abuse. And you are laying down everything here, unconditionally, youth and health and beauty and hope, and at twenty-two you will look like a woman of five-and-thirty, and you will be lucky if you are not diseased, pray to God for that! No doubt you are thinking now that you have a gay time and no work to do! Yet there is no work harder or more dreadful in the world or ever has been. One would think that the heart alone would be worn out with tears. And you won’t dare to say a word, not half a word when they drive you away from here; you will go away as though you were to blame. You will change to another house, then to a third, then somewhere else, till you come down at last to the Haymarket. There you will be beaten at every turn; that is good manners there, the visitors don’t know how to be friendly without beating you. You don’t believe that it is so hateful there? Go and look for yourself some time, you can see with your own eyes. Once, one New Year’s Day, I saw a woman at a door. They had turned her out as a joke, to give her a taste of the frost because she had been crying so much, and they shut the door behind her. At nine o’clock in the morning she was already quite drunk, dishevelled, half-naked, covered with bruises, her face was powdered, but she had a black-eye, blood was trickling from her nose and her teeth; some cabman had just given her a drubbing. You don’t believe that you will ever be like that? Do you see how it ended? But when you are dying, all will abandon you, all will turn away from you, for then there will be nothing to get from you. What’s more, they will reproach you for cumbering the place, for being so long over dying. However you beg you won’t get a drink of water without abuse: ‘Whenever are you going off, you nasty hussy, you won’t let us sleep with your moaning, you make the gentlemen sick. That’s true, I have heard such things said myself. They will thrust you dying into the filthiest corner in the cellar—in the damp and darkness; what will your thoughts be, lying there alone?
